figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), a novel architecture where the next executed transformer layer is chosen at runtime. We use strided window attention within the routed core to allow information to flow through the sequence dimension while using the same attention and MLP parameters for all tokens within each window.
figures.headline: The architecture picks the next transformer layer at runtime, using strided window attention within its routed core.
citing_sentences: We visualize our novel architecture in Figure 1.
We visualize our forward pass in Figures 1 and 2, and provide pseudocode in Algorithm 1 in the appendix.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and a top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of a prelude, a routed core, and a coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of $W$ tokens, and at every routed depth a router selects one layer from the shared library per window (top-left). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by $S$ tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window $0$ has no history, so its router uses the first token and a learned vector $e^{(\ell)}$ for routed depth $\ell$ (bottom-left). For window $i>0$, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows $0,\dots,i-1$ and selects one layer (bottom-right). With $W=4$ and $S=2$, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in a new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4.
figures.headline: Shifted window boundaries let information pass between neighboring windows, while each window uses one router-selected layer per depth.
citing_sentences: We build on these works by incorporating architectural choices from looped transformers, such as only using recurrence in the middle layers of the model; see Figure 2 (top-left).
We visualize our forward pass in Figures 1 and 2, and provide pseudocode in Algorithm 1 in the appendix.

For example, with $n=8$, $W=4$ and $S=2$, depth $1$ uses the windows $\{0,\ldots,3\}$ and $\{4,\ldots,7\}$, depth $2$ uses $\{0,1\}$, $\{2,\ldots,5\}$ and $\{6,7\}$, and depth $3$ goes back to the first split (Figure 2, top-right).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Library of Layers learns distinct paths for different languages and distinct strategies when solving sudoku puzzles and mazes. Left: PCA projection of the routing paths of a $360M$ parameter LoL model trained on an equal mixture of $10$ languages. We see the paths taken are distinct per language and Latin-script languages use similar paths. Middle and Right: We train $360M$ parameter LoL models to solve sudoku (middle) and mazes (right), using $5$ different strategies. We then force each strategy’s mode path at inference time and see the models use the correct strategy (algorithm) with close to $100\%$ accuracy.
figures.headline: Routing paths separate languages, and forcing each strategy's path makes the model use that sudoku or maze algorithm with close to 100% accuracy.
citing_sentences: In Figure 3 (left), we see that the routing paths are reasonably distinct per language and the Latin-script languages all share similar paths.
In Figure 3 (middle), we plot the confusion matrix where we force the mode path for each strategy.

Figure 3 (right) shows that forcing LoL to follow a particular computational path produces the requested algorithm’s trace with nearly $100\%$ accuracy, even when all strategies share the same output syntax.

abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

sections.body:
Transformer layers run in one fixed order for every input. The authors argue this may waste capacity, because useful primitives must be represented again at several depths. Prior work adds sparsity through mixture of experts (MoE) or reuses layers in looped models, but keeps the order fixed.

LoL instead uses a small router, trained end-to-end without explicit supervision, to select each next layer from a global library of transformer blocks. Library size sets the regime: a small library forces reuse, and a large library leaves many layers inactive on a given pass.

Routing each token separately causes attention mismatches, so the method uses windowed attention with window boundaries shifted across depths. The paper reports synthetic, multilingual, safety, and language modeling experiments.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fixed layer order limits transformers, so the paper proposes a router that picks each next layer from a shared library.

sections.body:
Looped transformers reuse the same blocks across depth. Mixture of experts layers route tokens among experts at a fixed position. Methods that add a skip option to the router let tokens bypass layers, and other work routes through multiple smaller transformer layers.

The closest prior work pretrains a model before adding layer reuse and uses top-k routing with k greater than one, where LoL uses top-1 routing.

LoL differs because each window selects a complete transformer block from a library shared across all routed depths. Both block ordering and block reuse therefore depend on the input.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior looped, skipping and mixture-of-experts designs keep layer order or parameter choices fixed, while LoL selects whole blocks per window.

sections.body:
The model has a fixed prelude and coda around a routed core. Library size $L$ counts the stored blocks, and core depth $D$ counts the block applications.

Tokens are chunked into windows of $W$ tokens. All tokens in a window share one expert, and attention is restricted to earlier tokens in that window. Window boundaries shift by $S$ tokens between depths, so information flows between neighboring windows.

A linear router scores each window using only the mean hidden state of earlier windows, which preserves causality. The first window uses a learned depth-specific vector and the first token. Training uses loss-free load balancing and Gaussian noise on router logits, and starts with a shallow core that grows toward depth $D$.
sections.heading: How to Learn the Order of a Forward Pass
sections.headline: Each window selects one library block per depth; shifted window boundaries keep attention causal, and depth grows during training.

sections.body:
The authors train 360M models on multilingual, safety, sudoku, and maze data, then study and intervene on routing paths.

Principal component analysis (PCA) of routing paths shows distinct paths per language, with Latin-script languages sharing similar paths. A ridge probe on router probabilities reaches a test AUROC of 0.92, and a sequence-level probe reaches 0.95.

Forcing the mode path of each sudoku or maze strategy makes the model use that strategy. At 1B parameters on math data, LoL is competitive with dense baselines on loss and on benchmark accuracy. Against a mixture-of-experts model, LoL's training loss is approximately 0.05 higher.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Learned routing paths separate languages and algorithms, and LoL stays competitive with dense, looped and mixture-of-experts baselines.

sections.body:
The discussion argues that LoL unifies dense, looped and mixture-of-experts behavior in one model family, selected by library size. The authors describe the work as an initial exploration and expect future designs to improve on it.

They list several directions: intervening on routing features in chat settings, which they leave as an open question; using a larger routed depth at inference than at training; and routing over a growing library of test-time learnable adapters instead of full blocks.

The stated goal is not only competitive performance but also a tool for interpretability and control of reasoning strategies.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors call this an initial exploration and propose controllability, test-time scaling and adapter routing as next steps.

sections.body:
Appendix A gives the architecture. The 360M models follow GPT-2 Medium with RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU MLPs and bias-free attention, and the 1B model follows the Llama-3.2-1b shape. It also describes loss-free load balancing and a learned depth-dependent scale and bias after each normalization.

Appendix B ablates growing, auxiliary-loss balancing, shared router weights and attention patterns. Appendix C reports safety readouts, where top-1 ridge reaches a development AUROC of 0.8754 and shuffled labels average 0.5014.

It also covers sudoku and maze dataset construction, strategy formats, evaluation metrics, and extended 1B benchmark results in Table 5.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists architecture and training details, ablations, extra benchmark tables, sudoku and maze data, and routing visualizations.
